newsitem.title: EGYPT: Palestinians start airline, but can't fly from home.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians start airline, but can't fly from home.

text.p: Jubilant Palestinian pilgrims inaugurated their "national" airline on Friday but had to take off from an Egyptian airport because Israel has blocked flights from Gaza.

"Today when I know I am flying on my airline, the Palestinian airline, I am happy, very happy," said Essam Younis Mohammad, before he and 95 other Palestinians boarded for the journey to Saudi Arabia.
"This is the first time I am flying on my airline."
The two Palestinian Airlines Fokker 50 planes took off into clear blue skies from Port Said Airport in northern Egypt early on the first day of the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan.

Hours later a Jeddah control tower operator told Reuters by telephone that the planes had landed in Saudi Arabia, completing the first regular flights by the Palestinian Authority's newly-established airline.
"Really, we are very happy. This is a historical moment for the Palestinians," said airline chairman Faiz Zaidan. "This is the first time the Palestinian Airlines makes its flights officially."
But Zaidan was also angry that Israel had blocked use of the airport the Palestinian Authority had built in the self-rule area of Gaza.

"This is a moment to blame the Israeli authorities," he said. "This is against the peace process, against Oslo agreements, We have the right to establish the airports and the airlines as the Palestinian Authority."
Men and women in headscarves waved red, green, white and black Palestinian flags as they walked onto the tarmac to board the white airplanes, trimmed with coloured stripes.

Some joyfully passengers showed reporters their boarding passes and luggage sporting stickers with the airline's circular logo. The pilgrims planned to perform the umra, or "minor pilgrimage", to the Moslem holy city of Mecca.

Zaidan said there would be five flights a week on the same Egypt-Saudi route, running Saturday, Sunday and Monday. The airline, wholly owned by the civil aviation authority of the Palestinian Authority, will bring Friday's pilgrims back between January 21 and 23.
The Palestinian Authority bought two second-hand Fokker 50 propeller jets from Fokker Aviation last May, the first aircraft for Palestinian Airlines.

Zaidan said Gaza airport itself has been allowed to receive only two flights -- one carrying Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, the other a Moroccan plane bringing aid for the Palestinians, Zaidan said.

"The Palestinian Airlines should at this moment be at Gaza airport," Zaidan said. "The main reason why Gaza airport is not operating is the Israeli side. Sooner or later this airport will be operated."
He said Palestinians were offering air traffic and security liaison offices to the Israelis to allay some of their security concerns.

Israel, which has overall security control of Arab territories it has occupied since 1967, allowed construction of the airport in self-ruled Gaza under a peace deal with Arafat but demands control. Palestinians must fly from Israel, Jordan or Egypt.
"We are human beings. Our people are human beings. Why should Palestinians come and spend 13 or 14 hours using a bus just to come and join their national airline?" Zaidan said.
